items.question: How many halvings make the bracket narrower than $10^{-9}$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the smallest $k$ with $2^k > 10^9$.

byKey.w9: Each halving gains one binary digit, not a decimal one.

explain.text: $2^{30} = 1{,}073{,}741{,}824 > 10^9$, so 30 halvings. Each one gains about 0.3 decimal digits.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the log of the later ratio by the log of the earlier one.

byKey.ratio: That is the first ratio of errors. The order compares the logs of two ratios.

explain.text: The ratios are $10^{-2}$ then $10^{-4}$, so $p = \ln 10^{-4} / \ln 10^{-2} = 2$. The digits double each step: Newton's signature.

items.prose: Computing $f'$ costs as much as computing $f$.
items.question: Which method gains digits fastest per evaluation?

options.why: Per evaluation Newton gains only $2^{1/2} = 1.414$, because each step costs two.
Bisection gains one bit per evaluation, far behind both.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count evaluations, not steps.

explain.text: Newton doubles the digits for two evaluations, $2^{1/2} \approx 1.414$ each. The secant method multiplies them by 1.618 for one. Newton wins back the lead only when $f'$ costs under about 0.44 of $f$.

items.prose: A safeguarded Newton solver has just evaluated $f$ at $\sigma = 0.3$, and its bracket is now $[0.3, 0.9]$. The Newton step would land at 2.53.
items.question: What does it do next?

options.text: Bisect: move to 0.6, the middle of the bracket

options.why: 2.53 is outside the bracket, so the safeguard refuses it.
The edge is not a better guess and can trap the method.
The bracket still holds a root, so the method carries on.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. A step outside the bracket is replaced by the midpoint.

explain.text: The Newton step leaves $[0.3, 0.9]$, so the solver bisects to 0.6. The bracket keeps the root and halves at each bisection. That is why the method always ends.

items.prose: Recall level 1: implied vol moves by about $\Delta V/\text{vega}$. A wing call has vega 0.0218 and is quoted to £0.0001.
items.question: How many vol points can a one-tick price error move its implied vol?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide £0.0001 by vega, then multiply by 100.

byKey.frac: That is the move as a decimal. Multiply by 100 for vol points.

explain.text: $0.0001 / 0.0218 \approx 0.0046$, which is 0.46 vol points per tick. The wing is ill-conditioned in absolute terms. A solver tolerance far below that chases noise.

items.prose: Runge's function $\tfrac{1}{1 + 25x^2}$ is interpolated at 21 equally spaced points of $[-1, 1]$.
items.question: What is the largest error, roughly?

options.why: That is the Chebyshev figure at $n = 20$. Equal spacing gives about 60.
That is $n = 10$. Doubling the points made it 30 times worse.
Between the end points it swings by about 60.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. On equal spacing the error grows with $n$.

explain.text: At $n = 20$ the equal-spacing error is 59.82, against 0.0177 on Chebyshev nodes. More equally spaced points make the end swings worse.

items.prose: Eleven equally spaced quotes have Lebesgue constant 29.9. Each quote is good to $\pm 0.002$.
items.question: What bounds the interpolant's error from the quotes alone?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the quote error by 29.9.

explain.text: $29.9 \times 0.002 = 0.0598$: errors in the quotes can grow thirtyfold between them. The Lebesgue constant is interpolation's condition number.

items.prose: A desk bumps only the 5-year quote of a natural cubic spline curve by 10 bp.
items.question: Which rates move?

options.text: Every rate along the curve, by amounts that fade with distance

options.why: The tridiagonal system links every $M_k$, so the whole curve moves.
The spline passes through every quote, so the curve near 5 years bends too.

options.text: None: the spline smooths the bump away
options.why: The spline still passes through the bumped quote exactly.

feedback.correct: All of them: a spline is global.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. One changed $y$ changes every $M_k$.

explain.text: The bump moved the 4-year rate 5.51 bp, the 8.5-year $-2.67$ bp and the 15-year $+3.25$ bp. Every second derivative depends on every quote. Local schemes exist for hedging.

items.prose: At 10 years a zero curve has $z = 4\%$ and slope $z' = 0.1\%$ per year.
items.question: What is the forward rate $f = z + tz'$ there?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add $t \times z'$ to $z$.

byKey.zero: That is the zero rate itself.

explain.text: $f = 4\% + 10 \times 0.1\% = 5\%$. A rising zero curve has forwards above it. Any kink in $z$ becomes a jump in $f$.

items.prose: You choose 9 points on $[-1, 1]$ for a degree-8 interpolant of a smooth function.
items.question: Which points?

options.why: Equal spacing gives Runge's swings at the ends.
That leaves the ends unconstrained, the worst place.
Where $f$ is zero says nothing about the node product.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Crowd the points towards the ends.

explain.text: Chebyshev nodes $\cos(k\pi/8)$ keep the node product level across $[-1, 1]$. For Runge's function at $n = 8$ they give error 0.2047 against 1.0452 on equal spacing.
